paper_title: When2Think: Learning Difficulty-Aware Length Control for Efficient Hybrid Reasoning Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve strong performance on complex tasks but exhibit systematic inefficiency: they often overthink easy problems and underthink hard ones. Existing approaches based on uniform length penalties or rigid routing incur an efficiency tax, trading reduced computation on easy instances for accuracy loss on hard instances. We formulate efficient reasoning as an instance-adaptive computation allocation problem and propose When2Think, a post-training framework for hybrid reasoning that dynamically allocates computation based on problem difficulty. Our method introduces Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), a reward-shaping mechanism that leverages pre-computed reference statistics (accuracy and token usage) to regulate reasoning depth. Combined with verifier-based rewards and batch-wise standardized advantages, IDAC enables stable critic-free optimization without learned reward models or online reference-model queries. When2Think encourages direct answering on easy instances while preserving extended reasoning on hard instances, thereby learning when to use System 1 (NoThink) versus System 2 (Think). Experiments on mathematical benchmarks demonstrate improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs: on AIME24, Pass@3 increases by 10.0% while token usage is reduced by 27.9% relative to the base model, and on AIME25, When2Think achieves 40.0% Pass@3, outperforming compression and routing-only baselines.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) [15] has transformed artificial intelligence (AI), enabling fluent and coherent text generation across wide range of tasks. However, many tasks of interest require not only fluent text generation but also reliable multi-step reasoning [6, 7]. prominent direction is to internalize structured reasoning capabilities through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) [810], producing large reasoning models (LRMs) that generate coherent reasoning trajectories and achieve strong performance on challenging benchmarks [1113]. Despite these advances, LRMs suffer from reasoning inefficiency [14]. They often overthink simple tasks by generating redundant reasoning tokens without accuracy gains [15, 16], yet underthink complex tasks by terminating reasoning prematurely or producing fragmented chains [17]. Static token-reduction strategies can further introduce an efficiency tax: suppressing overthinking on easy instances systematically harms performance on harder ones  (Table 1)  . We compare the When2Think (red), LRM baseline (blue) and LLM baseline (green). Lines: Mean Pass@1 accuracy standard deviation. Bars: Mean tokens per instance standard deviation. Statistics computed over five independent runs. When2Think mitigates the efficiency tax by selectively allocating computation across easy and hard instances. We adopt dual-process theory [18, 19] as conceptual lens for this mismatch. SYSTEM 1 denotes fast and intuitive responses, whereas SYSTEM 2 denotes slower and more deliberate reasoning [13]. Easy instances are often solvable with SYSTEM 1-style direct answering, while hard instances benefit from SYSTEM 2-style deliberation [20]. As shown in Figure 1, LLMs are efficient on easy instances, whereas LRMs allocate substantially more tokens to improve performance on harder ones. Motivated by these observations, we propose post-training framework for hybrid reasoning, combining the efficiency of SYSTEM 1-style direct answering with the deliberative power of SYSTEM 2-style reasoning in single model. We make the following contributions: Unified analysis of reasoning inefficiency. We analyze the efficiency tax ( 6.1), showing that token reduction reduces overthinking on easy instances but induces underthinking on hard ones. Reasoning as instance-adaptive control. We recast efficient reasoning as an instance-level adaptive control problem ( 6.2), shifting the focus from token reduction to difficulty-aware allocation. Adaptive hybrid reasoning via When2Think. We introduce When2Think ( 4), post-training method that uses Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC)-based reward shaping to control both whether to think and how much to think within unified hybrid reasoning policy. Figure 1 previews the behavior learned by When2Think, which achieves LLM-level efficiency on easy instances while preserving LRM-level accuracy on harder ones. When2Think shows the effectiveness of adaptive reasoning depth on the most challenging AIME benchmarks.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: We survey prior work on reducing reasoning cost in LRMs, focusing on post-training methods for efficient multi-step reasoning. Following recent surveys [14, 16], these approaches fall into two categories: (1) reasoning compression, which shortens intermediate reasoning traces, and (2) hybrid reasoning, which dynamically balances direct answers and explicit deliberation. Reasoning Compression. Reasoning compression aims to shorten reasoning trajectories while maintaining correctness. Data-level approaches, such as chunk-level distillation (Skip-Thinking [21]) and validity-aware selection (LC-R1 [22]), remove redundant steps from generated chains. Reinforcement-learning-based techniques introduce efficiency incentives via hard token budgets (ThinkPrune [23]) or reward-based length penalties (LASER [24], DLER [25]). These approaches effectively reduce overthinking on easy instances, but their static or globally tuned constraints can lead to underthinking on hard instances. 2 Hybrid Reasoning. Hybrid reasoning methods reduce computation by selectively applying reasoning. Reinforcement-learning approaches such as ARM [26] and LHRM [27] switch between short and long reasoning trajectories, while other methods (AdaptThink [28], ThinkLess [29]) skip reasoning on easy instances using learned controllers. Although these methods reduce overthinking or enable hybrid reasoning, they lack fine-grained, instance-level control. To address this limitation, we introduce When2Think, which unifies efficient SYSTEM 1 and deliberative SYSTEM 2 reasoning.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
sections.content: Post-training is one effective mechanism for encouraging SYSTEM 2-style reasoning in LLMs by modifying model parameters, leading to models commonly referred to as Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) or Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) [3034]. We focus on reinforcement learning (RL) approaches within the broader paradigm of learning to reason [8, 10, 35], which directly optimize reasoning policies to enhance both accuracy and efficiency [11, 12, 3638]. Additional reasoning paradigms for LLMs are discussed in G. Verifiable Rewards. Lambert et al. [39] introduce Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which replaces learned reward models with deterministic verification, directly aligning the RL objective with task correctness and reducing reward-model bias. Prior work [40, 41] uses verifiers either as Outcome-supervised Reward Models (ORMs) for final answers or Process-supervised Reward Models (PRMs) for step-level supervision, trading simplicity for annotation cost. RLVR leverages outcome-based verification to provide reliable rewards for multi-step reasoning without requiring step-level supervision. Importance Sampling. To mitigate cold-start bias and prevent premature collapse into the THINK mode, we adopt the importance sampling (IS) strategy of AdaptThink [28]. This IS scheme provides the hybrid reasoning setup used throughout training, while our contribution focuses on instanceadaptive control of reasoning depth. Hybrid reasoning is controlled by an explicit mode token (THINK or NOTHINK) prepended to each trajectory. When THINK is selected, explicit reasoning proceeds until designated end-of-thinking token (EOT); when NOTHINK is selected, the model skips deliberation and directly generates the final answer, similar to the NoThinking mechanism of Ma et al. [42]. sections.title: 4 When2Think
sections.content: We propose When2Think, post-training reward-shaping framework for adaptive computation allocation in hybrid reasoning. For each input, When2Think learns both whether to invoke explicit reasoning (THINK vs. NOTHINK) and how deeply to deliberate, dynamically balancing SYSTEM 1 direct answering and SYSTEM 2 multi-step reasoning. These behaviors are guided by offline reference statistics that estimate instance difficulty and expected reasoning cost (Figure 2). Rewards jointly favor correctness and efficiency. Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC) modulates correctness-gated efficiency bonus using trajectory length and pre-computed reference statistics: αi captures instance difficulty through reference accuracy, while τi estimates expected reasoning cost. The reward is normalized by the instance-specific baseline αi and standardized by BWS, enabling stable critic-free PPO-style optimization. Since correctness comes from verifiable rewards and reference statistics are pre-computed offline before each training epoch, training requires no learned reward model, learned critic, or online reference-model queries during policy updates.

sections.title: 5 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate whether this adaptive control maintains accuracy on difficult instances while reducing unnecessary computation on easier ones. Implementation details are provided in A.

sections.title: 5.1 Training
sections.content: We train When2Think on reasoning-capable base model, R1-distill-1.5B, compact language model distilled from DeepSeek-R1 [32] and built on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B [44]. The model was distilled using approximately 800k curated samples via SFT. Training is conducted on the DeepScaleR dataset [45], which contains approximately 40k competition-level mathematics problems with verified solutions. The dataset aggregates publicly available sources, including AIME (19842023), AMC (pre-2023), Omni-MATH [46], and Still [47], covering algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics.

sections.title: 5.2 Evaluation
sections.content: We evaluate models on diverse suite of mathematical reasoning benchmarks spanning gradeschool arithmetic, olympiad challenges, competition-level problems, and undergraduate STEM tasks, including GSM-Plus [48], OlympiadBench [49], AIME I/II (20242025), Minerva [50], and MATH500 [41]. Across these benchmarks, we evaluate models along two complementary dimensions: answer accuracy and token usage. Performance is measured using sampling-based pass@k [51], which reflects the probability that at least one of sampled outputs is correct. Efficiency is quantified by the average number of generated tokens per instance, computed independently of the pass@k sampling budget. Final answers are validated using dual-verifier strategy: predictions are deemed correct if accepted by either Math-Verify [52] or MARIO Eval [53], which together provide formatagnostic and type-aware symbolic and numerical equivalence checking. Further details of the evaluation settings are provided in B.

sections.title: 5.3 Baselines
sections.content: We evaluate When2Think against representative baselines from three categories: (1) base LLMs, (2) LRMs trained via SFT or RFT, and (3) efficiency-aware LRMs. We include both general-purpose and math-specialized LLMs, including Qwen2.5-Instruct [54] and Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct [44]. For explicit reasoning, we evaluate R1-Distill-Qwen [32], which also serves as the backbone of When2Think, and DeepScaleR-Preview [45], an trained on the same DeepScaleR dataset. We compare When2Think against representative efficiency-aware reasoning models. Length-compression baselines, including LC-R1 [22], ThinkPrune [23], and LASER [24], primarily reduce computation via global or heuristic length constraints. Hybrid reasoning baselines, such as AdaptThink [28] and ThinkLess [29], instead reduce cost by discretely skipping explicit reasoning on easier instances. All methods share the same base model and are trained under comparable conditions, ensuring that performance differences reflect the impact of adaptive reasoning rather than variations in model or supervision. For baselines that use the same training dataset [24, 28, 29], we follow their original data setup. All baseline models are implemented using open weights.

sections.title: 6.1 RQ1: Accuracy–Efficiency Trade-off under Adaptive Allocation
sections.content: We evaluate whether When2Think improves the accuracyefficiency trade-off by reducing unnecessary reasoning on easy instances without inducing under-allocation on hard ones. The Efficiency Tax. Many efficient reasoning methods reduce computation through fixed length constraints, heuristic compression, or discrete mode switching. While these strategies can suppress redundant reasoning on easy instances, they may incur an efficiency tax: token savings are obtained by removing reasoning that is still needed on harder instances. For example, on AIME24  (Table 1)  , LC-R1 and AdaptThink reduce inference cost relative to the R1-Distill-Qwen backbone, but their accuracy decreases by 10.0 and 1.3 points, respectively. similar hard-instance under-allocation pattern appears on MATH-500 Level 5 (Table 10 in C.3). Top-Right AccuracyEfficiency Improvements. Figure 6 shows the accuracyefficiency landscape across five benchmarks: GSM-Plus, Minerva, OlympiadBench, AIME24, and AIME25. Since the token axis is reversed, movement toward the top-right indicates better trade-off: higher accuracy with fewer tokens. Our claim is not that When2Think is always the lowest-token operating point; routing-only methods such as AdaptThink can be strong low-cost points on easier tasks. Rather, When2Think aims to reduce unnecessary computation without converting those savings into hard-instance accuracy loss. On AIME24, it reduces token usage by 3,959 tokens (27.9%) while improving accuracy from 46.0% to 56.0% (10.0%), showing that adaptive allocation can mitigate the efficiency tax rather than merely shift it.

sections.title: 6.2 RQ2: Difficulty-aware Adaptive Allocation between System 1 and 2
sections.content: We analyze whether When2Think dynamically allocates computation in difficulty-aware manner, balancing SYSTEM 1/2 across benchmarks of varying difficulty. SYSTEM 1 Preference on Easy Instances. On easy MATH-500 (Table 10 in C.3) Level 1 problems, the R1-Distill generates an average of 1,199 tokens despite minimal reasoning demand. In contrast, When2Think reduces token usage to 619 (580) while maintaining high accuracy (95.8%), indicating clear preference for SYSTEM 1-style direct answering when additional deliberation provides limited benefit. This pattern generalizes to easy GSM-Plus  (Table 1)  problems. SYSTEM 2 Engagement on Hard Instances. On hard MATH-500 (Table 10 in C.3) Level 5 problems, When2Think maintains accuracy while reducing token by 2,276 relative to R1-Distill, 7 indicating more selective yet sustained SYSTEM 2 reasoning. In contrast, on adversarially perturbed GSM-Plus instances, it deliberately increases computation (462 tokens), yielding 6.3% absolute accuracy gain. On long-horizon tasks such as AIME24/25  (Table 1)  , When2Think maintains sufficient deliberation depth, while compression-based and discrete hybrid methods often truncate reasoning prematurely, leading to poorer performance on hard instances. Instance-Level Difficulty-Aware Allocation. When2Think adapts reasoning behavior at the instance level. On MATH-500 (Figure 4 and C.2), the fraction of THINK trajectories increases monotonically with difficulty, from about 0.2 at Level 1 to over 0.7 at Level 5. By contrast, baselines exhibit weak or misaligned responses: ThinkLess allocates nearly constant computation, DeepScaleR overthinks easy instances, and AdaptThink under-allocates on hard ones. This demonstrates that When2Think more accurately matches computation to problem difficulty.

BWS stabilizes optimization. BWS converts IDAC-shaped trajectory rewards into standardized advantages, enabling stable critic-free optimization. Beyond variance reduction, it preserves cross-instance difficulty structure, allowing successful long trajectories on hard instances to receive positive credit. As shown in D.1 and D.2, BWS improves convergence, stabilizes response length and think ratio, and prevents degenerate reasoning behaviors, maintaining stable think ratio of approximately 0.9 compared to 0.6 without BWS (Figure 8). IS improves efficiency, not accuracy. Removing importance sampling (while retaining IDAC and BWS, Table 1) yields strong variant that outperforms DeepScaleR-Preview on most benchmarks, indicating that the primary accuracy gains stem from IDAC and BWS. However, IS shifts the policy toward more efficient operating point: compared with the w/o IS variant, the full When2Think model substantially reduces GSM-Plus token usage (1,652 1,052 tokens) while maintaining competitive accuracy. This suggests that IS primarily promotes effective NOTHINK usage on easier instances, rather than serving as the main source of accuracy gains ( D.3).

sections.title: 7.1 The Efficiency Tax: From Compression to Control
sections.content: We argue that reasoning efficiency in LRMs is better understood as an instance-adaptive control problem, rather than pure compression problem. Prior approaches reduce computation using static or heuristic length constraints, which suppress overthinking on easy instances but induce an efficiency tax by under-allocating reasoning on harder problems. This limitation suggests that inefficiency arises from misallocation of computation rather than insufficient model capacity. The strong performance of DeepScaleR-Preview further indicates that efficiency gains can emerge from improved allocation across instances, rather than compression alone. From Compression to Control. When2Think treats reasoning depth as an instance-adaptive resource, reallocating computation by suppressing redundant reasoning on easy problems while preserving or expanding deliberation on hard ones. This shifts the objective from minimizing reasoning length to optimizing where and how much reasoning is applied.

sections.title: 7.2 Mechanisms: Continuous Control and Stability
sections.content: IDAC is Necessary for Depth Allocation. While hybrid reasoning methods can learn when to invoke THINK, our results show that mode selection alone is insufficient. Removing IDAC while retaining balanced exploration and stable optimization leads to substantial drop in accuracy, particularly on hard benchmarks such as AIME24 (Figure 9 and D.3). Although such variants can still decide when to reason, they lack mechanism for determining how much reasoning to allocate, resulting in systematic under-allocation on difficult instances. These findings establish that difficulty-aware depth control is essential beyond discrete routing. When2Think implements this depth control through continuous modulation rather than discrete decisions. IDAC leverages instance-level statistics (αi, τi) to scale reasoning incentives, forming spectrum from direct answers to extended deliberation. This avoids abrupt truncation and enables instance-aware allocation of reasoning depth. Stable Optimization via BWS. Learning instance-adaptive control is challenging due to difficultydependent reward variability. When2Think addresses this with two mechanisms: instance-specific baselines αi, which eliminate the need for learned critic, and Batch-Wise Standardization (BWS), which normalizes advantages across the mini-batch. This decouples difficulty from optimization signals and enables stable, critic-free learning of length-sensitive policies.

sections.title: 7.3 The Paradox of Scale: Overthinking and the Visibility of Efficiency Tax
sections.content: Smaller reasoning models tend to generate longer but less effective reasoning traces, leading to systematic overthinking ( F). As result, inefficiencies such as the efficiency tax are most visible at smaller scales (Tables 9 and 10). Although When2Think generalizes to larger modelsmaintaining strong performance on hard problems while reducing unnecessary computationlarger models exhibit stronger inherent reasoning efficiency, making these effects substantially less pronounced. Accordingly, we focus our analysis on the 1.5B scale, where inefficient computation is most diagnostic and where adaptive control mechanisms such as IDAC have the greatest impact.

sections.title: 7.4 Limitations
sections.content: Our approach relies on verifiable rewards, and is thus most directly applicable to domains such as mathematical reasoning. Extending When2Think to open-ended tasks requires additional reward modeling or human evaluation. Moreover, our method depends on offline reference statistics for difficulty estimation, which may be less reliable when problem difficulty is ambiguous.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We argue that inefficiency in large reasoning models arises not from excessive reasoning, but from an efficiency tax caused by misallocated reasoning depth across instances. Existing approaches reduce 9 computation via static compression, but often do so at the cost of under-allocating reasoning on difficult problems. We propose When2Think, which treats reasoning depth as an instance-adaptive resource rather than quantity to be minimized. Through Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC), the model learns not only when to reason but how much to reason. Combined with BatchWise Standardization (BWS), this enables stable, critic-free optimization of depth-aware policies. Across diverse mathematical benchmarks, When2Think improves the accuracyefficiency trade-off by reducing unnecessary computation while preserving or expanding reasoning where it is needed. Overall, our results suggest that efficient reasoning is fundamentally problem of allocation rather than compression, providing principled direction for scalable reasoning systems.

sections.title: B Evaluation Setup
sections.content: B.1 Inference and Verification Protocol To ensure rigorous and reproducible evaluation, we standardize inference-time generation parameters and the answer verification pipeline across all models. Generation Configuration. We adopt decoding strategies tailored to the characteristics of each model class while keeping them fixed within each category for fair comparison. For general-purpose LLMs, we use temperature of 0.7 and top-p of 0.8 to encourage diverse solution exploration. For Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), we apply more deterministic configuration with temperature of 0.6 and top-p of 0.95, which stabilizes long-horizon reasoning while preserving sufficient diversity in intermediate steps. This distinction follows common practice in prior work and accounts for the differing sensitivity of LLMs and LRMs to sampling noise during reasoning, while all generation settings are held constant across benchmarks to ensure fair comparison. To ensure reliable answer extraction and automated evaluation, all models are instructed to follow strict output format using the system prompt shown in B.1, which is instantiated using each models native chat template.

sections.title: System Prompt for Mathematical Reasoning
sections.content: Math assistant. Provide step-by-step solution in English using LATEX. Final answer in boxed{...}. Answer Extraction and Verification. We report Pass@k accuracy based on answers extracted from the final boxed{...} tag. To ensure robustness to formatting variations and symbolic ambiguity, we employ Dual Math Verifier pipeline that integrates Math-Verify [52] and MARIO Eval [53]. Math-Verify performs primary extraction and symbolic equivalence checking, while MARIO Eval provides complementary semantic verification using type-specific Computer Algebra Systems (CAS). The resulting unified binary correctness signal is used consistently as both the evaluation metric and the terminal reward for policy optimization. B.2 Dual Math Verifier Accurate and robust verification is essential for evaluating mathematical reasoning and for constructing reliable reward signals during policy optimization. Because mathematically correct answers can be expressed in multiple symbolic or numerical forms, exact string matching is often insufficient. We therefore employ dual-verifier pipeline that evaluates semantic equivalence between model-generated answers and ground-truth solutions. Math-Verify. We use Math-Verify [52] as format-agnostic verifier for mathematical reasoning tasks. Given model-generated response, Math-Verify extracts the candidate answer using prioritized parsing rules that support diverse output formats, including LaTeX expressions and plain text. The extracted answer is then normalized and converted into symbolic representation, enabling comparison with the ground-truth solution beyond exact string matching. Verification is performed through symbolic equivalence checking and numerical evaluation with tolerance, allowing equivalent mathematical expressions to be recognized even when their surface forms differ. MARIO Eval. We additionally adopt MARIO Eval [53] to provide type-aware verification across diverse mathematical answer formats. MARIO Eval first identifies the answer type, such as scalar, algebraic expression, matrix, equation, or inequality, using rule-based parsing and optional languagemodel assistance when type inference is ambiguous. It then applies type-specific equivalence checks, primarily relying on symbolic computation through computer algebra system and numerical evaluation with tolerance. When symbolic verification is inconclusive due to structural ambiguity or natural-language formulations, MARIO Eval can optionally invoke math-capable language model as fallback judge. 18 B.3 Benchmarks We evaluate models on diverse suite of mathematical reasoning benchmarks spanning foundational arithmetic, intermediate competition problems, olympiad-level challenges, and undergraduate STEM tasks. Together, these benchmarks cover broad difficulty spectrum, enabling fine-grained analysis of both reasoning accuracy and computational efficiency across problem complexities. GSM-Plus. GSM-Plus [48] is medium-scale benchmark of approximately 10.5k problems that extends GSM-8K [40] with systematically perturbed variants. It introduces controlled modifications, including paraphrasing, numerical changes, distractor insertion, and reasoning-structure perturbations, enabling evaluation of robustness under increased reasoning complexity and distribution shift. Although GSM-Plus contains small number of instances annotated with None answers for unanswerable or incomplete cases, we exclude them to maintain consistent answer-extraction and verification protocol. This filtering yields final evaluation set of approximately 9k problems. MATH-500. The MATH-500 benchmark [41] is held-out evaluation subset derived from the original MATH [57] dataset, preserving its structure while avoiding contamination from the PRM800K [41] training pipeline. The full MATH dataset spans seven subjectsPrealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculusand assigns each problem difficulty level from 1 to 5 based on AoPS conventions, ranging from introductory AMC 8style problems to AIME-level items. To prevent overfitting due to inclusion of test-split MATH problems in PRM-800K, 500 uniformly sampled problems were isolated to form MATH-500. This subset retains the subject distribution and difficulty profile of the original test split, providing leakage-free benchmark for evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning. Minerva. The Undergraduate-Level STEM Problems, also known as the Minerva benchmark and referred to as OCW Courses in Lewkowycz et al. [50], consists of 272 self-contained problems collected from MIT OpenCourseWare materials across multiple STEM subjects, including SolidState Chemistry, Information and Entropy, Differential Equations, and Special Relativity. Each problem provides clearly delineated final answer and is automatically verifiable, either numerically (191 problems) or symbolically via SymPy (81 problems), emphasizing multi-step reasoning while excluding formal proofs or open-ended short answers. This benchmark is specifically designed to evaluate scientific and quantitative reasoning capabilities in large language models at the undergraduate level, bridging the gap between standard K-12 mathematics benchmarks and more advanced domain-specific problem-solving tasks. OlympiadBench-Math. OlympiadBench [49] is high-difficulty, bilingual benchmark comprising 8,476 problems across multiple STEM domains in both multimodal and text-only formats. For evaluation of mathematical reasoning, only text-only math problems are used to isolate multistep reasoning performance. Each problem includes an expert-verified solution, enabling reliable assessment of model reasoning. Experiments are conducted on curated subset of 674 open-ended, text-only English problems from the Math Competition track of OlympiadBench. AIME. The American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) is selective competition featuring integer-answer problems ranging from 000 to 999. These problems are substantially more challenging than standard AMC questions, requiring multi-step reasoning, careful case analysis, and deeper understanding of algebra, combinatorics, number theory, and geometry. For evaluation, both administrations (AIME and AIME II) are combined to form set of 30 problems. D Ablation Studies
sections.content: D.1 Reward and Advantage Landscapes under IDAC and BWS BWS versus GRPO in the Advantage Landscape. We analyze why Batch-Wise Standardization (BWS) is critical for optimizing IDAC by comparing three reward formulations: the raw THINK reward, BWS advantages, and GRPO-style group-relative advantages. We construct Monte Carlo simulation using offline statistics from R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B on DeepScaleR. For each problem, empirical accuracy α captures difficulty and reference length τ approximates typical reasoning cost. We then generate THINK trajectories by perturbing τ with log-normal noise and sampling correctness according to α. This setup isolates how different normalization schemes allocate credit to reasoning trajectories as function of problem difficulty and token usage. Figure 7: Empirically Grounded Advantage Landscape of Explicit Reasoning. Policy signals for simulated THINK trajectories constructed from R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B statistics on DeepScaleR. Colors represent reference accuracy α (hard problems in blue, α 0, to easy problems in yellow, α 1), and markers indicate correctness (circles for correct, crosses for incorrect). Left: Raw IDAC THINK reward with absolute length-sensitive bonus. Middle: BWS advantage (ours), which preserves positive advantages for long successful trajectories on hard problems. Right: GRPO-style advantage, where problem instance normalization yields fragmented signals and horizontal banding. BWS: Preserving Global Difficulty Signals. BWS converts raw IDAC rewards into relative advantages computed over the full mini-batch, rather than normalizing within each instance. This batch-wise formulation preserves cross-instance difficulty structure that is lost under instance-local normalization. As result, trajectories that solve difficult problems can remain above the batch expectation and receive positive advantages, even when their absolute rewards are reduced. As shown in Figure 7, this effect is most evident for low-α instances, where successful long trajectories retain positive optimization signals despite high token usage. Thus, BWS does not merely reduce variance; it preserves global difficulty signals in the advantage function, enabling credit assignment for deliberate but necessary long-horizon reasoning. GRPO: Removing Cross-Instance Reward Structure. In contrast, GRPO-style normalization computes advantages relative only to rollouts of the same problem, removing any cross-instance reward comparisons. While this eliminates instance-level scale variation, it also discards the global difficulty structure encoded in IDAC. As consequence, the advantage landscape becomes fragmented, manifesting as horizontal bands in Figure 7. Because normalization is restricted to within-problem rollouts, credit assignment becomes sensitive to the composition of sampled trajectories. In particular, long but successful reasoning traces on difficult problems may receive weak or unstable signals when competing against short incorrect or prematurely terminated rollouts. These results highlight key limitation of instance-local normalization, and motivate BWS as mechanism for preserving cross-instance difficulty structure in critic-free optimization. D.2 Analysis of BWS Training Dynamics We analyze training dynamics to evaluate the effectiveness of our optimization strategy, focusing on the role of Batch-Wise Standardization (BWS). Figure 8 reports both task performance and reasoning behavior throughout post-training. Improved Convergence and Stability. BWS substantially stabilizes policy optimization. Without BWS, raw reward signals exhibit high variance across instances, leading to noisy gradient estimates and unstable learning trajectories. By normalizing rewards using batch-level statistics (µk, σk), BWS reduces gradient variance and disentangles instance difficulty from policy quality in the optimization signal. This effect is particularly pronounced on AIME24, where problem difficulty varies sharply; under BWS, the model consistently improves performance even on the hardest instances. Controlled Reasoning Depth. BWS also plays critical role in regulating reasoning length. Without proper normalization, baseline policies tend to drift toward degenerate behaviorseither collapsing to minimal reasoning or producing excessively verbose outputsdue to unstable credit assignment. In contrast, When2Think maintains stable Think Ratio and Response Length, gradually adapting reasoning depth to optimize the accuracyefficiency trade-off. Notably, this behavior emerges without relying on an explicit value function, indicating that BWS effectively stabilizes critic-free policy optimization. Sample Efficiency and Difficulty Scaling. Our approach exhibits improved sample efficiency. On AIME24, When2Think reaches peak performance in approximately half the training steps required by the baseline. Moreover, the performance gap widens as task difficulty increases, highlighting robustness under high-entropy reasoning regimes. Finally, BWS decouples response length from accuracy, preventing the reasoning bloat observed in the baseline, where additional tokens fail to yield meaningful performance gains. Figure 8: Training Dynamics under Batch-Wise Standardization Ablations. When2Think (red, with batch-wise standardized advantage) and Baseline (blue, without standardization) on DeepScaleR. Top: GSM8K (easy). Bottom: AIME24 (hard). Each row reports validation accuracy, average token usage, and Think Ratio over training steps. 27 D.3 Analysis of IS & IDAC Training Dynamics We further analyze the roles of importance sampling (IS) and Instance-level Difficulty-Aware Control (IDAC) during training. We compare three variants: the full When2Think model, variant without IS (retaining IDAC and BWS), and variant without IDAC (retaining IS and BWS). This ablation isolates whether the observed accuracyefficiency trade-offs are driven by balanced THINK/NOTHINK exploration (via IS) or by difficulty-aware reward shaping and normalized optimization signals (via IDAC and BWS). IDAC and BWS provide the main depth-control signal. The IDAC+BWS variant removes the balanced exploration distribution induced by IS, while retaining difficulty-aware reward shaping and batch-wise standardized advantages. As shown in Figure 9, this variant remains competitive in validation accuracy, especially on the harder AIME24 benchmark. This suggests that the main depth-control signal is primarily driven by IDAC-based reward shaping together with BWS-based advantage standardization, rather than by importance sampling alone. IS shifts the policy toward more efficient hybrid operating point. Although IS is not the primary source of the depth-control signal, it changes the operating point of the learned policy. On the easier GSM8K benchmark, the full When2Think model achieves comparable validation accuracy while reducing both token usage and Think Ratio relative to the IDAC+BWS variant. This indicates that IS helps expose and exploit the NOTHINK mode during training, encouraging more efficient behavior when explicit reasoning is unnecessary. IDAC is necessary for difficulty-aware depth control. The IS+BWS variant retains balanced mode exploration but removes IDAC. While this variant can still learn to switch between THINK and NOTHINK, it lacks the difficulty-aware signal that determines how much reasoning should be allocated once THINK is selected. As result, IS alone can encourage mode switching, but does not provide the same control over reasoning depth across easy and hard instances. Figure 9: Training Dynamics under IS, IDAC Ablations. Training dynamics of three variants on DeepScaleR: the full When2Think model (IS + IDAC + BWS), variant without importance sampling (IDAC + BWS), and variant without IDAC (IS + BWS). Top: GSM8K (easy). Bottom: AIME24 (hard). Each row reports validation accuracy, token usage, and Think Ratio over training steps. 28 D.4 Ablation on Hybrid Bonus Design Separate bonuses provide limited benefit. As shown in Figure 10, varying the NOTHINK bonus η does not yield clear improvement in the accuracyefficiency trade-off. In particular, configurations with larger η tend to produce lower validation accuracy, suggesting that overly strong incentives for NOTHINK can bias the policy toward direct answering even when explicit reasoning remains useful. This behavior is consistent with hard-instance under-allocation: encouraging NOTHINK too aggressively can suppress necessary long-horizon reasoning. Figure 10: Training Dynamics under η and δ Variations. Training dynamics of When2Think under different η settings on DeepScaleR, with δ fixed to 0.05. Top: GSM8K (easy). Bottom: AIME24 (hard). Each row reports validation accuracy, token usage, and Think Ratio over training steps. Unified bonus yields more stable training. We therefore simplify the reward by using single correctness-gated efficiency coefficient δ for both modes, with DADS controlling how strongly the bonus is applied to THINK trajectories. The training dynamics in Figure 11 show that smaller unified bonus values lead to more stable behavior, avoiding both excessive NOTHINK collapse and overly verbose THINK trajectories. This suggests that the reward does not require separate mode-specific bonus coefficients. Figure 11: Training Dynamics under δ Variations. Training dynamics of When2Think under different efficiency-bonus coefficients δ on DeepScaleR. Top: GSM8K (easy). Bottom: AIME24 (hard). Each row reports validation accuracy, token usage, and Think Ratio over training steps. 29 D.5 Effectiveness of the Dual Math Verifier We analyze the contribution of the Dual Math Verifier through subject-level performance on MATH500. Figure 12 compares the Base Model (R1-Distill), the Baseline with standard verification, and our proposed method (Improved). Figure 12(c) further confirms that each subject exhibits sufficient coverage in both problem count and difficulty distribution, enabling meaningful comparison. Robustness to Non-Numeric Answers. Subjects such as Geometry and Precalculus contain high proportion of symbolic, structured, or text-heavy answers. In these categories, the Baseline exhibits notable performance degradation due to the inherent limitations of string-based verification, which fails to recognize semantically equivalent but syntactically distinct solutions (e.g., reordered vector coordinates or algebraically equivalent expressions). By incorporating symbolic equivalence checking, the Dual Math Verifier effectively resolves this mismatch, substantially improving robustness to non-numeric answer formats and yielding consistent gains across these subjects. Trade-offs in Intermediate Algebra. Performance gains in Intermediate Algebra are comparatively smaller. This behavior is not attributable to data scarcity, as models such as DeepScaleRtrained on the same datasetachieve stronger results, but rather reflects trade-off between verification strictness and recall. In particular, complex multi-step derivations involving alternative but equivalent forms (e.g., factored versus expanded polynomials) may be falsely rejected under strict symbolic parsing. Moreover, efficiency constraints imposed by IDAC can limit the allocation of reasoning steps required for such transformations. These observations suggest that subject-aware verification tolerance or adaptive length modulation may further improve performance in algebra-intensive domains. sections.title: F Problem Characterization
sections.content: F.1 Impact of Model Scale and Supervision on Reasoning Efficiency We examine reasoning efficiency across model scale and supervision using the Olmo-3 [60] family (7B and 32B). Figure 17 shows the accuracytoken usage trade-off across model scales, post-training strategies (SFT vs. RFT), and reasoning paradigms (standard LLMs vs. LRMs). The results highlight systematic inefficiencies in current post-training approaches and illustrate how model capacity and supervision affect reasoning cost. The Paradox of Scale: Smaller Models Overthink. Figure 17 reveals clear paradox of scale in reasoning efficiency. Smaller 7B models are concentrated in the high token-usage regime relative to 32B models, despite achieving substantially lower accuracy. This indicates that limited model capacity is associated with inefficient and prolonged reasoning trajectories, phenomenon referred to as capability-induced overthinking. In contrast, 32B models achieve higher accuracy with fewer tokens, exhibiting superior reasoning economy. similar trend is observed in the R1-distill family  (Table 9)  , suggesting that stronger base capabilities enable more direct and efficient problem-solving paths. The Cost of Reinforcement Learning. Figure 17 shows consistent efficiency tax under Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT). Within the same model scale, RFT models (hollow markers) are systematically shifted toward higher token usage compared to their Supervised Fine-Tuned (SFT) counterparts (filled markers). These shifts are accompanied by only modest accuracy gains, resulting in less favorable accuracytoken trade-off. This behavior is consistent with outcome-based reinforcement learning objectives that do not explicitly penalize token usage, leading to longer chain-of-thought generations across instances. Overall, RFT models occupy Pareto-inferior region relative to SFT baselines. The Mechanics of Inefficiency: Why RLVR Inflates Tokens. The token inflation observed in RFT modelsparticularly those trained with RLVR [39], such as OlmoRL [60]follows directly from the optimization objective. Unlike SFT, which imitates concise human-curated reasoning traces, RLVR optimizes only for outcome correctness and imposes no explicit constraint on token usage. The absence of KL regularization term further permits substantial deviation from the SFT initialization. Consequently, longer reasoning trajectories become favorable strategy for increasing success probability. Without explicit difficulty-aware control, RLVR therefore tends to produce inefficient and overly verbose reasoning behavior. sections.title: G Paradigms
sections.content: G.1 Dual Process Theory in LLMs. The dual-process theory of cognition [18, 61] posits two distinct modes of reasoning: System 1, which is fast, intuitive, and heuristic-driven, and System 2, which is slow, deliberate, and analytical. This framework has been increasingly applied to understand reasoning in language models [13]. Within this perspective, approaches for enhancing model reasoning can be interpreted as attempts to either simulate or internalize System 2 capabilities. G.2 Inference-Time Scaling for System 2 Simulation Inference-time scaling strategies allocate additional computational resources at inference to elicit deeper reasoning from pre-trained models without modifying their parameters [11, 13, 62]. Common techniques include: Prompting methods: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [63], Plan-and-Solve [64], Self-Refine [65], Self-Consistency (SC) [66]; Structured search methods: Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) [67], Stream-of-Search (SoS) [68], Adaptive-Parallel-Reasoning (APR) [69]; Other strategies: self-evaluation, external tool use, or retrieval-augmented reasoning [11]. These methods simulate System 2-like reasoning through external guidance, but can incur substantial computational overhead and may produce unnecessarily long or inefficient reasoning trajectories. G.3 Post-Training for Reasoning In contrast, post-training approaches aim to internalize analytical reasoning capabilities by updating the models parameters. This paradigm, often called learning to reason [8, 10, 35], aligns model weights with reasoning-specific objectives during dedicated post-training phase [13]. Learning to Reason. Typically, general-purpose LLMs are adapted through: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on step-by-step rationales [70], which aligns the model to produce coherent reasoning steps. Reinforcement learning (RL) to reward coherent multi-step trajectories [11, 12, 3638], encouraging models to internalize structured reasoning behavior. Knowledge distillation [7173], transferring reasoning capabilities from expert models to smaller or general-purpose LLMs. Models resulting from this processfrequently termed Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) or Reasoning Language Models (RLMs) [3034]are explicitly optimized for structured reasoning rather than fluent text generation alone. Search to Learn. Recent work integrates search-based strategies into the training loop to refine reasoning trajectories used for fine-tuning. For example, Retro-Search [58] retrospectively revises suboptimal paths using an MCTS-inspired algorithm, while other methods employ MCTS [74] or self-exploration [75, 76] to generate step-level feedback guiding models toward more deliberate reasoning. Collectively, search-enhanced post-training methods shift supervision from outcome-focused objectives toward optimization of the reasoning process itself. Post-training therefore provides pathway to internalize System 2-like capabilities, though at the cost of longer training cycles, increased data curation requirements, and potential generalization limitations to unseen reasoning tasks.

sections.title: H Extended Discussion
sections.content: H.1 Broader Impacts The proposed method addresses the efficiency of reasoning in large language models by treating computation as an instance-adaptive resource rather than quantity to be globally minimized. Potential positive societal impacts include reduced computational and energy costs for deploying reasoningcapable models, which may lower barriers to access in research and educational settings with limited resources. Improved efficiency may also facilitate more predictable reasoning behavior by reducing unnecessary or unstable long-horizon reasoning on simple inputs. At the same time, improving the efficiency of reasoning models may reduce the cost of deploying automated systems in real-world decision-making contexts. If such systems are used without appropriate verification or human oversight, incorrect or biased reasoning could lead to harmful outcomes, particularly outside domains with clear ground-truth verification. Our work partially mitigates this risk by focusing on verifiable mathematical reasoning tasks; however, extending similar techniques to open-ended or socially sensitive domains would require additional safeguards, such as domain-specific validation, conservative deployment practices, or human-in-the-loop monitoring.
